newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: Zaire peace talks move to secret SAfrican location.
newsitem.headline: Zaire peace talks move to secret SAfrican location.

text.p: Zaire's civil war factions were likely to meet at a secret location in South Africa on Sunday to discuss peace terms after fresh rebel gains overshadowed a preliminary meeting and dimmed prospects for a quick ceasefire.
A rebel spokesman expressed exasperation about Saturday's unexplained delay in starting substantive talks and said he was uncertain when the two sides would sit down together.

The rebels, who now control of over a third of the vast country and can negotiate from a position of strength, have said they will not stick around for talks if they feel the Zaire government is not acting in good faith.
They insist that President Mobutu Sese Seko, who has ruled Zaire for 32 years, must step down.
South Africa, which is facilitating the talks, declined to give any details about their location. There was unconfirmed speculation that they would take place somewhere outside Pretoria.
The negotiating process got off to a shaky start, coinciding with news that rebel forces had overrun the diamond centre of Mbuji-Mayi in central Zaire and were greeted by cheers from residents.
The advance left them poised to march on to Lubumbashi, Zaire's second city, in mineral-rich Shaba province.
The rebels bristled at allegations that they had refused to allow international relief agencies to help about 100,000 Rwandan refugees on territory they control.

They said the charges were inspired by enemies including France, long a Mobutu ally, and, in an apparent challenge, they gave authorisation to the United Nations to begin a massive -- and very expensive -- rescue airlift.
At his Goma headquarters, rebel leader Laurent Kabila rubbed salt in government wounds by taking a march-past by 400 re-educated former government soldiers.
In Pretoria, the two sides met at a frosty ceremony on Saturday in the South African cabinet chambers.
After short speeches, there was a chill handshake between Zairean Foreign Minister Kamanda wa Kamanda and Bizima Karaha of Kabila's rebel alliance.
The negotiators then parted and were later moved to a secret location outside Pretoria to get down to business. But by nightfall talks had still not started.
"I won't speculate. I simply do not know," Karaha said. "We may start talking tonight or it may not be until tomorrow."
In his blunt opening speech, Karaha underlined the widespread view that it was rebel victories and Kabila's mounting popularity that forced the government into negotiations.
"We are here because those brothers of ours have realised for the first time they can't make it with mercenaries and genociders. They can only make it with us if they still want to survive," he said.
